name: Neverver
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: Stress is not phonemically contrastive. A purely auditory analysis suggests that primary stress is assigned to the penultimate syllable of polysyllabic lexical stems and falls on the single syllable of monosyllabic stems. When lexical items contain more than one stem, stress is assigned separately to each stem. [p. 96] ... In each item in (2.105) above, the common noun prefix is counted in the assignment of stress. [p. 97] ... 2.7.2. Stress assignment in verbs. Stress falls on first syllable of the verb stem, regardless of the shape of the subject/mood prefix. The prefix, which is obligatorily attached to verb stems, is disregarded in the assignment of stress. [p. 98]
new_statements.citation: Barbour, Julie Renee. 2009. A grammar of the Neverver language of Malakula (Vanuatu). PhD thesis, University of Waikato. §2.7 Stress, pp. 96-98.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-contrastive and stem-based: primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of a polysyllabic lexical stem (monosyllables stressed on their only syllable). In nouns the fossilised common-noun prefix n(V)- counts as part of the stem, e.g. [ˈni.jo] 'water', [ni.ˈte.rix] 'child'. In verbs the obligatory subject/mood prefix is excluded and stress falls on the first syllable of the verb stem ([imˈвulem] '(s)he will come', [nit.ˈmal.ma.lu] 'we dispersed'); reduplicated stems are stressed on their first syllable. Every stem in a compound gets its own stress ([ˈniliβ-ˈmaβus], [ne.ˈɣel.ˈβas] 'four-legged creature').
new_statements.secondary_stress: No secondary stress described; compounds and multi-stem words carry a primary stress on each stem; the post-verbal negative particle si 'carries stress, although it is normally not stressed as strongly as the stress-carrying syllable of the verb' (ch. on negation).
new_statements.exceptions: Verb rule: stress on stem-initial syllable, prefix disregarded (so trisyllabic stems like malmalu are stressed on the antepenult of the stem); footnote 16: the vowel-initial stem /is/ 'be bad' is monosyllabic with singular realis prefixes and the whole inflected syllable bears stress [ˈis]. Imperatives: additional stress on the subject/mood prefix ([ˈkam.ˈtuɸ] 'go away!'), distinguishing imperative from plain irrealis.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (lexical stems, including affixed nouns and inflected verbs); based on a 'purely auditory analysis' of corpus and elicited speech, no instrumental study. Separate §2.8 covers intonation.
new_statements.identity_note: Same variety as ling1265: Barbour describes the Neverver spoken in Limap and Lingarakh villages, north-central Malakula (c. 560 speakers), which she says is based on the Mindu dialect; the historical Sakhan dialect is lost and no synchronic dialect differences are treated (thesis §1.1, pp. 4-6). No other named variety involved.

sources.note: Stress not contrastive; primary stress on the penultimate syllable of polysyllabic lexical stems (noun prefix counted), on the sole syllable of monosyllables; each stem in a compound stressed separately; in verbs stress on the first syllable of the verb stem, subject/mood prefix disregarded (exception: vowel-initial stem /is/ 'be bad'); reduplicated stems stressed on first syllable; imperatives carry an extra stress on the prefix. Auditory analysis only. Followed by §2.8 Intonation patterns pp. 99-102.

No stress rule given.
